[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is that of a subacute-to-progressive, multifocal neurodegenerative syndrome with prominent cerebellar (gait ataxia, dysarthria), brainstem (dysarthria, likely oculomotor/bulbar involvement implied by brainstem atrophy), and basal ganglia (urinary incontinence — often early autonomic feature; possible subtle parkinsonism not yet documented) involvement. The timeline is key: urinary incontinence for 1 year, followed by progressive gait ataxia leading to wheelchair dependence over 1 month — indicating *subacute acceleration* of a previously smoldering process. This pattern — early autonomic dysfunction (urinary incontinence) preceding or co-occurring with cerebellar and brainstem signs — strongly favors multiple system atrophy (MSA), particularly the cerebellar-predominant (MSA-C) or mixed (MSA-C/P) subtype. MSA is defined by α-synuclein pathology affecting oligodendroglial cells, leading to combined autonomic failure, cerebellar ataxia, and/or parkinsonism. MRI findings of atrophy and signal abnormalities in the brainstem (e.g., “hot cross bun” sign), cerebellum, and basal ganglia are highly characteristic of MSA-C/MSA-P and distinguish it from most hereditary ataxias (which typically spare basal ganglia early and lack prominent autonomic failure) and autoimmune or mitochondrial disorders (which rarely show this specific tri-regional atrophy/signal pattern without additional systemic or metabolic clues). Prion disease is less likely given absence of rapid progression (<6 months), myoclonus, cognitive decline, or DWI hyperintensity — all notably *not mentioned*, and progression is described as “subacute, progressive”, not fulminant. While genetic ataxias (e.g., SCA2, SCA3) can have autonomic features, urinary incontinence is uncommon as an *early isolated* symptom — more typical is late-stage bladder dysfunction. Friedreich ataxia is excluded by adult onset (urinary incontinence for 1 year, wheelchair dependence at subacute pace — inconsistent with FRDA’s childhood/adolescent onset and slower progression) and lack of areflexia, scoliosis, or cardiomyopathy. Autoimmune ataxia (e.g., anti-GAD65) usually presents with isolated cerebellar syndrome, not brainstem/basal ganglia atrophy or early incontinence. Mitochondrial disorders would more likely show lactate elevation, stroke-like episodes (MELAS), or basal ganglia T2 hyperintensity with symmetric necrosis (Leigh), none of which are reported. NBIA typically presents with dystonia-parkinsonism and iron accumulation on SWI/T2*, not cerebellar atrophy or early incontinence. Thus, MSA remains the single most coherent diagnosis integrating *temporal evolution*, *anatomic distribution*, and *clinical phenotype*.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Subacute, progressive gait ataxia resulting in wheelchair dependence over 1 month  
- Urinary incontinence present for 1 year — early and prominent autonomic dysfunction  
- New-onset dysarthria — indicating brainstem (pontine/cerebellar outflow) involvement  
- Brain and cervical spine MRI shows atrophy and signal abnormalities in brainstem, cerebellum, *and* basal ganglia — a tri-regional pattern highly characteristic of MSA  
- No subjective sensory loss — argues against Friedreich ataxia and many hereditary SCAs with sensory neuropathy  
- No overt pyramidal signs reported — makes primary lateral sclerosis or HSP less likely  
- Absence of rapid progression, myoclonus, or cognitive decline makes prion disease unlikely per standard criteria  

[GAPS]  
- Autonomic testing results (e.g., orthostatic hypotension, urodynamics, cardiac MIBG) not yet performed  
- Detailed exam findings: presence/absence of parkinsonism (rigidity, bradykinesia), ocular pursuit deficits, nystagmus, stridor, or inspiratory sighs — not specified  
- MRI-specific sequences: absence/presence of “hot cross bun” sign (pons), putaminal rim hyperintensity or atrophy, or diffusion restriction — not detailed in summary  
- CSF neurofilament light chain (elevated in MSA vs. low in many genetic ataxias) — pending  
- Genetic testing results (SCA, FXN) — pending  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Multiple system atrophy (MSA-C or MSA-P)

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is that of a subacute-to-progressive, multifocal neurodegenerative syndrome with prominent cerebellar (gait ataxia, dysarthria), brainstem (dysarthria, likely oculomotor/bulbar involvement implied by brainstem atrophy), and basal ganglia (urinary incontinence — often early autonomic feature; possible subtle parkinsonism not yet documented) involvement. The timeline is key: urinary incontinence for 1 year, followed by progressive gait ataxia leading to wheelchair dependence over 1 month — indicating *subacute acceleration* of a previously smoldering process. This pattern — early autonomic dysfunction (urinary incontinence) preceding or co-occurring with cerebellar and brainstem signs — strongly favors multiple system atrophy (MSA), particularly the cerebellar-predominant (MSA-C) or mixed (MSA-C/P) subtype. MSA is defined by α-synuclein pathology affecting oligodendroglial cells, leading to combined autonomic failure, cerebellar ataxia, and/or parkinsonism. MRI findings of atrophy and signal abnormalities in the brainstem (e.g., “hot cross bun” sign), cerebellum, and basal ganglia are highly characteristic of MSA-C/MSA-P and distinguish it from most hereditary ataxias (which typically spare basal ganglia early and lack prominent autonomic failure) and autoimmune or mitochondrial disorders (which rarely show this specific tri-regional atrophy/signal pattern without additional systemic or metabolic clues). Prion disease is less likely given absence of rapid progression (<6 months), myoclonus, cognitive decline, or DWI hyperintensity — all notably *not mentioned*, and progression is described as “subacute, progressive”, not fulminant. While genetic ataxias (e.g., SCA2, SCA3) can have autonomic features, urinary incontinence is uncommon as an *early isolated* symptom — more typical is late-stage bladder dysfunction. Friedreich ataxia is excluded by adult onset (urinary incontinence for 1 year, wheelchair dependence at subacute pace — inconsistent with FRDA’s childhood/adolescent onset and slower progression) and lack of areflexia, scoliosis, or cardiomyopathy. Autoimmune ataxia (e.g., anti-GAD65) usually presents with isolated cerebellar syndrome, not brainstem/basal ganglia atrophy or early incontinence. Mitochondrial disorders would more likely show lactate elevation, stroke-like episodes (MELAS), or basal ganglia T2 hyperintensity with symmetric necrosis (Leigh), none of which are reported. NBIA typically presents with dystonia-parkinsonism and iron accumulation on SWI/T2*, not cerebellar atrophy or early incontinence. Thus, MSA remains the single most coherent diagnosis integrating *temporal evolution*, *anatomic distribution*, and *clinical phenotype*.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Subacute, progressive gait ataxia resulting in wheelchair dependence over 1 month  
- Urinary incontinence present for 1 year — early and prominent autonomic dysfunction  
- New-onset dysarthria — indicating brainstem (pontine/cerebellar outflow) involvement  
- Brain and cervical spine MRI shows atrophy and signal abnormalities in brainstem, cerebellum, *and* basal ganglia — a tri-regional pattern highly characteristic of MSA  
- No subjective sensory loss — argues against Friedreich ataxia and many hereditary SCAs with sensory neuropathy  
- No overt pyramidal signs reported — makes primary lateral sclerosis or HSP less likely  
- Absence of rapid progression, myoclonus, or cognitive decline makes prion disease unlikely per standard criteria
